title: How Porta-Potties Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how porta potties work, covering the history from World War II shipyard and bomber toilets (the Andy Gump, the Elson chemical toilet) through fiberglass "Strong Box" units, polyethylene models, roll-around toilets, and luxury restroom trailers ("honey wagons"). They describe the modern servicing process (vacuum-pumping waste into a truck and dumping it at a treatment plant), the blue dye, fragrances, and enzyme-based biocides that replaced formaldehyde, freezing problems in winter, and the hazards of servicing units, including tipped-over units. The episode opens with a promo for SF Sketch Fest and closes with a listener mail correction about John Cleese's surname pronunciation and Carol Cleveland's omission.

segments.title: Sketch Fest promo and episode introduction
segments.summary: Josh promotes the hosts' San Francisco Sketch Fest show in January, then introduces the episode on porta potties and jokes about the gross subject matter.

segments.title: Taste of Chicago porta potty logistics
segments.summary: Discussion of the Taste of Chicago festival in Grant Park, with roughly 380 porta potties, 28 wheelchair-accessible units and 80 handwashing stations supplied by Service Sanitation, Inc., and the nightly servicing schedule that kept them usable.

segments.title: How servicing works and porta potty trade culture
segments.summary: The hosts explain that servicing trucks vacuum waste from units into a tank and dump it at a municipal waste treatment plant. They mention the trade magazine Portable Restroom Operator and funny company slogans such as Got To Go and There's no one takes care of our business like Mr. John.

segments.title: World War II origins: shipyard and bomber toilets
segments.summary: Origin stories of portable toilets begin with shipbuilding at Long Beach during World War II, where workers built temporary toilets aboard ships. Bomber crews also needed toilets on long flights, leading to relief tubes, produce crates, and the Elson chemical toilet.

segments.title: Elson toilet problems and pilot accounts
segments.summary: Quotes from fighter pilots describe the Elson toilet spilling contents during turbulence and the discomfort of using it. A story is told about pilots dropping Elson toilets on German targets.

segments.title: Outhouses versus porta potties and public health
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish outhouses, which are permanent structures over holes, from self-contained porta potties that hold waste. They argue porta potties benefit public health and save water.

segments.title: Evolution: Strong Box, fiberglass, polyethylene, and ventilation
segments.summary: George Harding's patent for a portable toilet cabana with a vent pipe is discussed, along with Harvey Heather's fiberglass Strong Box, its drawbacks (dark, not stackable, fragile, absorbs odor), and the shift to polyethylene units made in assembled parts.

segments.title: Roll-around toilets, luxury restroom trailers, and honey wagons
segments.summary: Crane-liftable and roll-around toilets for multi-story construction are described, followed by luxury restroom trailers (honey wagons) with running water and porcelain toilets, first built in 1954 by Porta John in Columbus, Ohio.

segments.title: Inside a porta potty: blue dye, fragrance, and biocides
segments.summary: The hosts explain that blue dye hides waste, fragrance additives mask odor, and biocides evolved from formaldehyde to beneficial enzymes and microbes that break down waste and toilet paper. Warm weather speeds bacterial activity.

segments.title: Freezing waste, servicing hazards, and tipped-over units
segments.summary: Frozen waste in winter is discussed, including brine mixtures and rock salt cakes in urinals. The hosts describe the difficulties of servicing units, found objects such as phones and wallets, and the worst case of a unit tipping onto its door.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on porta potty workers
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck encourage listeners to thank porta potty service workers, noting the job's public health role and water savings.

segments.title: Listener mail: John Cleese pronunciation and Carol Cleveland
segments.summary: A listener notes that John Cleese's name rhymes with cheese, his father changed the spelling from Cheese, and the hosts apologize for omitting Carol Cleveland from the Monty Python episode.
